transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-08-23 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (BlueHarbor CTO), Ethan Cole (Head of ML), Simon Park (Security)

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough of Redwood model catalog, Demo of selecting open models for two regulated medical workloads (radiology report summarization + patient triage chat), discussion of benchmarks, compatibility matrix (quantization, kernel/hardware fit), and regulatory concerns (data residency, KMS, SOC2). Agreed to run an on-prem pilot for a small radiology inference path.

Topics:
- Redwood Console model catalog navigation
- Benchmarks: latency/cost tradeoffs and template
- Serving modes: Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security: SOC2/ISO, KMS, audit logs, data residency
- Next steps & pilot scoping

Action items (abbreviated):
- Diego to prepare benchmark configs and cost delta for two workloads
- Maya to share compliance artifacts and KMS integration notes
- Priya to confirm dataset and legal POC

Questions noted:
- How does caching affect PHI exposure?
- What are the live failover patterns between Dedicated and Hosted?
- Can we run a private on-prem control plane in an air-gapped environment?

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. Diego is our solutions engineer, he'll do most of the console walkthrough. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya here. Thanks.
[00:15] Ethan: Ethan on the call.
[00:17] Simon: Simon Park joining from security.
[00:20] Diego: Great, thanks. We'll jump into a quick agenda and then i'll share my screen.
[00:30] Maya: The goal here is to show how you'd pick open models from the catalog, run bench's, and then decide host vs dedicated vs privet. Sorry, privet private is often mis-typo'd in our docs but it's the Private offering.
[00:45] Diego: Alright i'm sharing the Redwood Console. You can see the model catalog on the left, we've pre-filtered by 'open models' and by 'medical-likely' tag — that tag is just a curation hint, not a compliance guarantee.
[01:10] Ethan: Quick q — how do you ensure models aren't leaking PII during inference or caching?
[01:18] Diego: Good one. We have automatic prefix and KV cache controls. By default we disable persistent caching for PHI sensitive routes. There's also token redaction hooks you can enable server-side. Note: some earlier notes in our docs call it KV cash which is just a transcription thing.
[01:40] Maya: And from a deployment perspective, for regulated data we usually recommend Redwood Private with customer-managed KMS; or Redwood Dedictaed in a VPC with restricted egress.
[01:55] Simon: What's the difference from a security posture between Dedicated and Private?
[02:00] Diego: Main diff is control plane. Dedicated is still hosted by Redwood but you get reserved GPU pools, VPC peering, and stricter logging. Private gives you the option for a customer-controlled control plane and on-prem agents — that's the route for air-gapped or full data residency.
[02:25] Priya: For BlueHarbor we need to keep all PHI in-country and prefer customer keying for KMS. Is that supported?
[02:34] Maya: Yes, customer-managed keys and HSM integrations are supported on Private. For Dedicated we can offer bring-your-own-key with limited controls — Diego can detail the options.
[02:45] Diego: Absolutely. I'll pull up the compatibility matrix now — this shows model size, supported quantization profiles, kernel mapping (NVIDIA A100 vs H100 vs CPU optimized), and recommended deployment mode.
[03:05] Diego: Here we have a 7B open model that scores well on radiology summarization in our bench sprints; it's fast with 8-bit quant and maps well to A100 and the newer H100 kernels for low latency.
[03:30] Ethan: Are those bench results run with our prompts or Redwood's internal prompts?
[03:35] Diego: The catalog example is our internal baseline prompts. For your pilot we'd run the same bench harness with your promptset and sample documents so the numbers reflect your workload.
[03:50] Maya: We also have Optimize suggestions: batching, cache rules, and quant profiles that show expected cost per 1k tokens and latency percentiles.
[04:05] Simon: How do you handle audit logs? We need immutable logs for all admin operations and model changes for compliance.
[04:13] Diego: Audit logs are available across modes. For Private we ship logs to your SIEM via S3 or syslog; Dedicated we push them into a partitioned storage with strict retention and optional WORM setting. There's a small note in the security pack about retention SLOs.
[04:35] Priya: Can you show the benchmark template? We want to validate latency at P95 < 150ms for the triage chat and cost under a threshold.
[04:45] Diego: Sure. Opening the bench tab — here's the benchmark template we use. Fields are: model, sequence length/cutoffs, batch profile, hardware target, tokenization spec, and prompt set. For triage chat we usually include 128-tok context with a 32 token response median.
[05:10] Diego: If we run on H100 with 8-bit quant and a continuous-batching policy, we expect median latency around 80-110ms for a 7B model; P95 will depend on concurrency and batching window but we can tune it.
[05:30] Ethan: What's the cost delta between hosted and dedicated for steady throughput?
[05:36] Maya: Hosted is usage-based and generally cheaper for small volume bursty workloads. Dedicated reduces unit cost at committed throughput — once you commit to sustained traffic the per-token cost falls significantly. Diego will give an estimate.
[05:50] Diego: I'll add a sample calc: for 100k tokens/day triage, hosted might be X (we'll send a concrete estimate) while dedicated committed capacity can be 30-40% lower per-token depending on GPU and quantization.
[06:05] Simon: We also need to ensure model lineage: which weights were used, model provenance. Is that in the catalog?
[06:12] Diego: Yes each catalog entry includes provenance — model hash, source hub link, and a vetted-flag if we've run the compatibility bench. Small caveat: automatic vetting is best-effort and we surface known caveats (e.g., hallucination rates on clinical datasets).
[06:35] Priya: On hallucinations — do you have any evals for clinical accuracy?
[06:41] Diego: We run accuracy evals when customers provide labeled sets. For out-of-the-box catalog models we publish generic bench signals; for clinical use we'd run your curated eval suite as part of the pilot.
[06:56] Maya: Ok let's demo a shortlist flow — Diego, could you search for models that meet our constraints: open-license, supported for on-prem, 8-bit quantable, and good small-context summarization scores?
[07:10] Diego: Filtering now... here's a shortlist of three: Open-Radiant-7B (caveat: tokenizer differences), MedLight-7B (community fork), and LibriMed-6.7B. Note some names are community aliases and can be spelled differently in upstreams.
[07:32] Ethan: MedLight looks promising — what's the kernel map?
[07:35] Diego: MedLight maps to optimized fused-attention kernels on H100 and has a fast NVFuser path on A100. For CPU fallback it's heavier but workable for very low QPS.
[07:50] Simon: Regarding data residency, if we run Dedicated with VPC peering to our private subnet, does any inference traffic leave region?
[07:59] Diego: No — traffic routing can be restricted; for Dedicated we can lock down egress to your region. For Hosted there are regional endpoints but they are still Redwood-managed. Private gives you full network control on-prem.
[08:15] Priya: We have an internal compliance blackout for moving PHI to third parties. Likely Private. How long to spin up a Private instance for a small pilot?
[08:24] Maya: Typical timeline is 2-4 weeks for Private in a standard case — shorter if we use the lightweight on-prem agent installer; longer if air-gapped setup and legal paperwork. We'll need your infra and security contacts for the onboarding runbook.
[08:40] Ethan: On performance benches, do you support mixed-precision or advanced quant like GPTQ?
[08:46] Diego: We support several quant profiles including INT8 and GPTQ-styled post-training quant. The catalog flags whether a model has a robust quantized execution path. Sometimes the model needs a recompile for best kernel mapping — that's part of our bench pipeline.
[09:10] Maya: I'm going to open the Optimize tab briefly: Optimize surfaces the recommended batching window, cache rules, and a suggested quant profile with expected unit cost. It also shows historical regressions if you pin a model version.
[09:28] Diego: For example, here's Optimize recommending an 8ms batching window for chat-like workloads to improve throughput while staying under latency SLO.
[09:40] Priya: That sounds risky for triage — we need deterministic latency. Can you set hard latency caps?
[09:47] Diego: Yes — we support SLO policies that cap batching latency and can fallback to a lighter model variant if the window is exceeded. We call it graceful degradation: model variant routing and auto-fallback.
[10:05] Ethan: Good. Can you also show how we would run our own bench harness?
[10:10] Diego: Sure, under Bench -> Import we have a template CSV. You'll fill: prompt_id, prompt_text, expected_response_length, and reference label. We run async benches and return P50/P95/token counts, and a bench report with raw logs.
[10:35] Simon: A few security nitty-gritty: are private keys ever retained by Redwood? What's key rotation look like?
[10:42] Diego: With customer-managed keys on Private, Redwood never holds the private keys. Rotation is handled by your KMS; for Dedicated with BYOK we have a trust boundary and short-lived key tokens — we can detail in the security doc.
[11:00] Priya: We need to ensure that model artifacts loaded on GPU are not exfiltrated. Any protections there?
[11:07] Diego: On Private we can restrict access to the host, use disk encryption, and enforce hardware breakout policies. For Dedicated we run in a hardened tenant, but it's not the same as your on-prem attestation.
[11:25] Maya: Let me pause — sounds like Private is likely. What if we start with a short Dedicated PoC to get numbers while parallelizing the Private onboarding?
[11:35] Priya: That could work. We'd want the same model and configs so numbers are comparable.
[11:40] Diego: Yes we can pin the model version and run bench suites across both environments. We'll capture the kernel maps and quant profiles used so it's reproducible.
[12:00] Ethan: Any gotchas on tokenizer mismatches when moving between environments? We've seen production drift because of tokenization differences.
[12:06] Diego: We track tokenizer version and tokenization artifacts in the catalog entry. It's a common source of drift; we include a standard tokenization checksum in the model metadata.
[12:25] Priya: Let's talk about cost targets — we have a rough target to keep inference cost below $0.02 per patient-interaction. Is that realistic?
[12:34] Maya: It's doable depending on model choice and quant. With a 6-7B quantized model and dedicated capacity it's plausible. We'll run scenarios in the estimate.
[12:50] Diego: I'll put an example calc in the follow-up sheet: tokens per interaction estimate, quantization gain, and GPU amortization.
[13:00] Maya: Quick note — we've seen customers choose a two-model pattern: a smaller fast model for triage and a larger model for deeper summarization. That helps with cost/latency balance.
[13:15] Ethan: Yeah that matches our internal thinking.
[13:18] Diego: Returning to the compatibility matrix — here's the exportable CSV. We can attach this to the pilot ticket.
[13:30] Simon: On the legal side, what does the DPA/BAA look like? We need a BAA for PHI.
[13:36] Maya: Redwood offers a BAA for enterprise contracts; we'll send the template. For Private deployments the BAA covers only the control plane if managed; for on-prem deployments it's more about the support scope.
[13:55] Priya: Ok, so next steps from our side: confirm pilot dataset, and legal will review the BAA. From Redwood: security pack and bench template.
[14:05] Maya: Perfect. Diego — anything else to demo?
[14:08] Diego: I'll run a short live bench example with a canned triage prompt set to show the report format. Running now — this will take ~30s.
[14:30] [pause as Diego runs bench]
[15:05] Diego: Results are in. P50 92ms, P95 184ms on hosted H100 with 8-bit quant — note this is baseline with our sample prompts. We'll attach raw logs.
[15:22] Ethan: P95 184 is higher than our 150 target, but with tuning and dedicated it's probably doable.
[15:30] Diego: Right, with a narrower batching window and model variant we can push P95 down; and dedicated with H100-optimized kernels tends to improve tail latencies.
[15:45] Simon: Will you capture the exact kernel versions and runtime flags used in the bench report?
[15:49] Diego: Yes the bench report includes kernel name, driver versions, and the exact runtime flags. Sometimes those show up as slight typos in the UI (e.g., NVfuser spelled NVFuser or nv-fuser) — but the logs are exact.
[16:05] Maya: Switching gears — procurement question: if we move from Dedicated to Private later, what happens to reserved capacity commitments?
[16:12] Diego: That's contractual; typically commitments are handled on a case-by-case basis. We can structure the contract to allow credits toward Private onboarding. We'll have legal map that out.
[16:30] Priya: For the pilot, we'd like a cost/latency report comparing hosted vs dedicated vs private for two workloads, plus a security appendix.
[16:38] Maya: Understood. We'll send that.
[16:42] Diego: One more feature: routing policies. You can route by policy: e.g. prefer Private if SAML token indicates 'sensitive=true', else fallback to Dedicated. This allows mixed-mode operational safety.
[16:55] Ethan: Nice. How are rollouts handled? We need canary rules for model updates.
[17:00] Diego: Rollouts are built-in: percentage traffic, A/B tests, and automatic rollback on quality regression (we can wire your eval sets into the regression monitors).
[17:20] Simon: Ok, that's helpful. Two compliance questions remaining: where are audit logs stored and for how long? And can we retain them beyond standard retention?
[17:30] Diego: Logs can be exported to your S3 with lifecycle rules; retention is configurable and we can support extended retention and immutable settings for Dedicated/Private.
[17:45] Priya: Final question on monitoring: does Redwood expose model-level quality signals (like hallucination alerts) in the Console?
[17:53] Diego: Yes, quality monitoring can be tied to eval sets. We emit regression alerts with a diff view and link to offending prompts. It's part of Optimize.
[18:10] Maya: Great. Quick recap and next steps?
[18:14] Priya: We'll confirm dataset and internal POC lead.
[18:18] Maya: Redwood will send SOC2/ISO pack, bench template, and a pilotsheet with estimated costs. Diego will prepare bench configs comparing hosted/dedicated/private and run an initial on-prem feasibility note.
[18:30] Ethan: Sounds good.
[18:33] Simon: we'll review the BAA and get back.
[18:36] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the attachments.
[18:40] Priya: Thanks all.
[18:42] Maya: Bye.

References:
